anya: Heads-up — I landed a change yesterday and perf CI flagged a host-side regression. p95 end-to-end increased ~10-15% for short requests. Quick profiling points to tokenization + request parsing + streaming chunk flushes. attaching notes below.

mike: Oof. Which path is dominating? tokenize or JSON parse?

anya: tokenize (about 40%) + req-parsing (20%) + grpc/http framing overhead (15%). KV cache lookups negligible. I ran a flamegraph on a 1k requests sample.

jordan: can you paste the hot stack?

anya: ```
# top functions by cpu% (host preprocess)
tokenizer::tokenize_bytes  38.4%
json_parser::parse_body     19.7%
http::frame::read_headers  10.8%
streaming::chunk_writer    9.2%
grpc::metadata_unpack      6.1%
other                      15.8%
```

lee: tokenizer at 38% is surprising — we thought most tokenization moved to wasm JIT. Is this on the dedicated runtime host path?

anya: This is host-side preproc before we hand tokens to the runtime: client is sending raw text, we still run a light normalize/tokenize stage (mainly whitespace normalization + token offsets) so runtime can reuse KV cache correctly. That step is single-threaded per request today.

sam: Do we have numbers on p50/p95 breakdown mapping to those stages?

anya: Quick table: p50 total 12.6ms -> preproc 2.4ms; p95 total 45.1ms -> preproc 8.4ms. After micro-optimizations (compiled tokenizer) we get p95 preproc ~3.0ms in dev box.

mike: What about request parsing? Are we doing full JSON parse for every request? Could we do streaming partial parse or use simdjson?

anya: We're using serde_json currently, full parse to validate router fields + tool-calls. Tried a simdjson experiment: parsing time dropped ~60% in the bench, but integration risk (error reporting different).

jordan: For streaming chunking: are we flushing on newline or byte count? If chunk_writer is hot, maybe we're doing tiny writes.

anya: We flush on every 512 bytes currently. But many responses are under that and we do an extra metadata write for headers then a small chunk, which hits the syscall path. batching heuristics could flush at 2x size or coalesce for first N chunks.

lee: gRPC costs look non-trivial — metadata_unpack at 6%. Could be repeated per message for streaming. Does the client attach tracing metadata every message?

sam: Yes, we noticed some SDKs re-send per-chunk metadata. We added a short-term fix in SDK to avoid per-chunk metadata (just send at stream start). Would help both HTTP/2 and gRPC.

mike: Actionable ideas: (1) swap serde_json -> simdjson for host path (feature flag), (2) replace tokenizer with compiled lookup table + SIMD for common cases, (3) change chunk flush policy to coalesce small writes for first 64ms or until payload > X bytes, (4) add a lightweight tokenized client option where SDK sends pre-tokenized offsets.

jordan: Also consider async preproc threadpool so host accept path is not blocked; hand off CPU-bound tokenization to worker pool, return placeholder to runtime when ready. That helps short p50 latencies.

anya: I prototyped (1) and (3) on dev box: simdjson reduces parse stage from 8ms -> 3ms for 99th percentile; coalescing flushed small writes cut syscall rate by ~45% and reduced tail by ~6%. Combined p95 improved from 45ms -> ~28ms in dev.

lee: Nice. Risks? simdjson license? error messages? portability on ARM?

anya: simdjson is MIT, seems fine. ARM has lower wins but still better than serde in my bench. Error shape differs, we can map errors to existing schema.

sam: For SDK pre-tokenize: we need to standardize token format (byte offsets + model id). That's more invasive but best long-term p50 win. Could be opt-in.

mike: One more regression note: kernel selection appears unaffected; these are strictly host-side costs before model execution begins. But host overhead can push requests across batching boundaries in runtime (we're seeing more 1-sample batches because host latency increased), so it's indirectly causing GPU efficiency regressions too.

jordan: Good catch — so host fix reduces both CPU latency and improves batching heuristics downstream. We should measure batch size distribution before/after.

anya: I already captured a snapshot: avg batch size among short requests dropped from 3.8 -> 2.9 after the regression. After my prototype fixes it goes back to ~4.1.

lee: Next steps?

mike: Let's do a small rollout: feature-flag simdjson + coalesce flush in canary cluster, run perf CI, and monitor batch size distribution, p50/p95 end-to-end, and GPU token throughput. Keep SDK pre-tokenize as a parallel spike.

anya: I can open a PR with the simdjson switch + flush heuristics behind flags. Will include a benchmark harness and comparison logs. tagging @deploy-bot for canary deploy once merged.

deploy-bot: build #3826 passed, queued for canary deploy to cluster-02. :rocket:

sam: Thanks — can you also add a CI job that reports host preproc p50/p95 and batch size histograms? Splitting out stages in the perf report will help catch regressions.

anya: Yup will add. I'll post follow-up thread with PR link and before/after numbers.

mike: thumbs up. :thumbsup:
